title: Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)
summary: Describes the Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm, a modern way to create and verify digital signatures. It gives parameters for the edwards25519 and edwards448 curves, with an example implementation and test vectors.

plainLanguage.summary: EdDSA is a method for creating a digital signature that others can check with a public key. This RFC specifies versions based on two Edwards curves and gives code examples and test data so implementations can agree on the result.

questions: what is the difference between ed25519 and ed448
how big is an ed25519 signature
subtitle: Two Edwards-curve signature schemes with fixed parameters, implementation guidance, and test vectors.

tldr.problem: Implementations need a precise, interoperable way to create and verify digital signatures using Edwards curves.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8032 defines EdDSA and five parameter sets based on edwards25519 and edwards448, including key encoding, signing, verification, example code, and test vectors.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It recommends Ed25519 when its security level is sufficient and Ed448 otherwise.

today: RFC 8032 is an Informational RFC from the IRTF. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Benefits
sections.content:
The Edwards-curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA) is a variant of Schnorr's signature system that uses Edwards curves. RFC 8032 gives recommended parameters for edwards25519 and edwards448, an implementation-oriented description, example code, and test vectors.

The RFC describes high performance across platforms, small keys and signatures, and complete curve formulas that avoid exceptions for valid points. EdDSA derives its signing value from the private key and message, so it does not need a fresh random number for every signature. Its collision-resilience claim applies only to PureEdDSA.
sections.plainLanguage: EdDSA lets a signer prove that a message came from a particular private key. Its fixed curve choices and test vectors help different implementations produce and check compatible signatures.

sections.title: The EdDSA Design
sections.content:
The general EdDSA description has eleven parameters, including a prime field, a curve, a base point, a hash function, and a prehash function. The RFC says implementations should use a defined parameter set such as Ed25519 or Ed448 rather than implement the general form directly.

A private key is hashed to derive a secret scalar and additional signing data. The public key encodes the curve point made by multiplying the base point by that scalar. The complete addition formulas work for all points on the curve, with no exceptional cases.
sections.plainLanguage: An implementation chooses a specified set of curve and hash parameters. It derives a public key from the private key, but the public key does not reveal that private key.

sections.title: Signing and Verifying
sections.content:
A signature contains the encoded point R followed by the encoded integer S. The signer hashes the private-key material and message to derive a value r, computes R as a multiple of the base point, then computes S modulo the group order. This makes signatures deterministic for the same key and message.

To verify, the receiver decodes the public key, R, and S. The receiver rejects invalid encodings or an S outside the permitted range, then checks the curve's group equation. The signature is valid only when that equation holds for the supplied message and public key.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer computes a signature from the private key and the message. The receiver checks a mathematical relation using the public key; a signature for a different message will not pass that check.

sections.title: The Ed25519 and Ed448 Variants
sections.content:
The RFC defines five parameter sets: Ed25519, Ed25519ctx, Ed25519ph, Ed448, and Ed448ph. PureEdDSA signs the message directly and requires two passes over it. HashEdDSA first applies a prehash, which supports a single-pass signing interface but does not retain PureEdDSA's collision-resilience property.

Ed25519 uses 32-octet public keys and 64-octet signatures. Ed448 uses 57-octet public keys and 114-octet signatures. Contexts can distinguish protocol uses; where allowed, the signer and verifier must use identical context bytes, and the maximum context length is 255 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: Ed25519 and Ed448 use different key and signature sizes. The context variants add a shared label to the signing process, while the prehash variants hash the message first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Signatures are deterministic, which avoids failures caused by poor per-signature randomness. Private-key generation still requires randomness. Implementations can reduce side-channel leaks by using the same instructions and memory accesses for every private key; the example code in the RFC does not provide that protection.

The verification check that S is less than the group order prevents signature malleability. The RFC recommends Ed25519 if its nominal 128-bit strength is enough and Ed448 otherwise. It says the prehash variants SHOULD NOT be used, and advises against signing large messages when the receiver cannot buffer them before verification.
sections.plainLanguage: Implementations must protect private keys and avoid operations whose timing or memory use reveals them. The RFC also explains that deterministic signing removes one source of random-number failure, but key creation still needs randomness.
